title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meeting in the Middle ⚡
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS launches two simultaneous BFS searches—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. This “meeting in the middle” strategy can dramatically reduce the number of explored nodes for faster shortest-path routing.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half — how two simultaneous searches can double traversal speed ⚡

Here’s the city-map visualization: we start BFS from Camden (start) and another BFS from your destination, expanding layer-by-layer like two teams sprinting toward each other. When the frontiers intersect, we reconstruct the shortest path immediately—no need to flood the whole graph.

Deep technical breakdown (quick but real):
• Standard BFS: explores outward from start, branching grows fast → big search space.
• Bidirectional BFS: runs BFS(start) and BFS(goal) in parallel.
• Key idea: for many graphs, the distance to the meeting point is about half the shortest-path length, so explored nodes shrink from ~b^d to about 2·b^(d/2).
• Implementation detail: use two queues, two visited maps (or distances), and stop as soon as a node appears in both visited sets.
• Path recovery: store parent pointers from both sides, then stitch at the meeting node.

Takeaway: If the graph is unweighted and you need the shortest path, Bidirectional BFS is a high-leverage graph optimization—especially when the goal is known.

Debate question: Would you rather guarantee early exit (bidirectional) or keep the simpler single-direction BFS? 🤔
